title: Is there any other fold that matches a square?
description: After the four known folds of a square, other folds are tried to see whether any more make the halves overlap. Keeko doubts that a fold from a corner to the middle of a side would match.
teaching_notes: One idea: a square has exactly four matching folds and no others. Watch for students who think any neat-looking fold through a corner also works.

source: Is there any other way to fold the square so that the two halves overlap? How many lines of symmetry does the square shape have?
video_script.why: The child learns that the four known folds are all there are, and counts them.
video_script.substitution: Try other folds on the square after the four known ones and see whether the halves overlap.
video_script.anchor: A square with its four known folds drawn, and one other fold tried
video_script.wrong_answer: a fold from a corner to the middle of a side also matches
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says a fold from a corner to the middle of the opposite side also makes the halves overlap. Folding it shows one corner sticking out, so the idea is struck out.

final_answer.spoken: no other fold works, and a square has four lines of symmetry

never_show: a count before the folds are tried
a tick on the other fold
maths_rules: A line of symmetry is a fold line along which one half covers the other exactly.
The four known folds of a square: straight down, straight across, and the two corner to corner folds.
A fold from a corner to the middle of a side leaves a corner sticking out, so it does not match.
A tilted fold through the centre at any other angle does not match either.
A square has exactly four lines of symmetry.
video_script.design: One idea: the four known folds are all there are. Assumes the child has found the four folds of a square. The square with its folds stays on the board from the hook to the end.
